metadata.title: Why did Micron stock fall 13% on Friday and should you buy the dip?

content.text:
Investing.com -- Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU) stock tumbled more than 13% on Friday, extending a brutal two-session decline that has now erased a portion of the stock's parabolic year-to-date run.
Broadcom's fiscal Q2 2026 earnings report released the prior Thursday evening, in which CEO Hock Tan did not raise the company's full-year AI semiconductor revenue target, sparked a sector-wide reassessment of whether AI infrastructure spending is beginning to plateau — a narrative that strikes at the very heart of Micron's premium valuation.
However, this was not the only driver behind Micron's poor performance on Friday.
Why did Micron stock fell on Friday?
A sharp selloff in Micron shares could be an early warning sign of the market impact from the upcoming SpaceX IPO, according to BNP Paribas equity derivatives strategist Greg Boutle.
Micron, one of the most popular stocks among retail investors, was the worst performer in the S&P 500 with the Friday selloff marking its biggest one-day decline since April 2025.
Boutle noted that Micron was the most-bought stock by retail investors over the past month, suggesting the stock's weakness may reflect investors beginning to free up capital ahead of the highly anticipated SpaceX listing.
"If retail investors want to buy SpaceX, they have a lot of PnL but not necessarily a lot of cash, which means they might have to sell other stock to make room for SpaceX," Boutle said.
The strategist has previously described the SpaceX IPO as potentially "the summer's most important market catalyst," arguing that the transaction could trigger significant portfolio repositioning among both retail and passive investors.
In an earlier note, Boutle warned that "selling flows in recent winners and levered products from retail to invest in SpaceX could be very large," as investors seek to raise funds to participate in the offering.
He estimates that retail and passive investors together could sell $50 billion or more of equities to fund purchases of SpaceX shares. The impact could be amplified if leveraged ETFs are forced to reduce exposure, creating what he described as a disproportionate amount of market delta to be sold and potentially triggering additional mechanical rebalancing flows.
Boutle also pointed out that passive buying related to SpaceX is expected to occur close to quarter-end, potentially coinciding with broader portfolio adjustments.
Beyond the IPO itself, he sees the potential for "a massive more than $100 billion U.S. equity selling flow, unrelated to the SpaceX IPO" during the quarter as investors rebalance portfolios following the strong outperformance of U.S. equities relative to fixed income.
Nvidia fears resurfacing
Compounding the damage, media reports surfaced suggesting that Nvidia may reduce the standard memory configuration for its Rubin NVL72 computing platform, potentially cutting total memory capacity per rack by roughly half. This raised immediate concerns about future HBM demand volumes, the highest-margin product in Micron's portfolio.
Adding to the bearish backdrop, filings showed 65 discretionary transactions between March and June consisting entirely of sales, reinforced caution ahead of Micron's own fiscal Q3 earnings report scheduled for June 24.
A notable piece of positive news — Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's confirmation in Seoul on June 5 that Micron, alongside Samsung and SK Hynix, had been certified to supply HBM4 memory for the next-generation Vera Rubin AI platform — failed to arrest the decline, as investors appeared to view the certification as already priced into the stock.
The broader market provided no relief: the NASDAQ dropped 4.2% and the S&P 500 fell 2.6%, while the PHLX semiconductor index suffered its worst single-day loss in six years on June 5. A stronger-than-expected May jobs report — 172,000 nonfarm payrolls added versus an 80,000 forecast — further stoked fears of Federal Reserve rate hikes, adding macro headwinds to an already pressured tech sector.
Should investors buy the dip in Micron stock?
Historically, periods of tight memory supply have been supportive for Micron's earnings and margins. The current cycle differs from previous memory booms because demand is increasingly being driven by AI data centers rather than consumer electronics.
"While the share price and multiple continue to reach new highs, we note limited pushback among the investor base; there's a general understanding that it really is "different this time,", Raymond James analyst Melissa Fairbanks said earlier this week.
AI-related demand is consuming a growing share of global memory production, contributing to shortages across parts of the memory market and prompting concerns from industries ranging from autos to telecommunications.
Micron has said supply constraints could persist beyond 2026, while several industry reports indicate that the company's HBM supply for next year is already sold out. That backdrop suggests the long-term investment debate remains centered on the durability of the AI memory cycle rather than on the recent share-price volatility.
"Not only have all suppliers been more rational in capacity additions, the industry also has never seen a similar demand environment, with a significant (understatement of the year) investment being made by multiple customers at the same time," Fairbanks added.
